7040261d8ba1a395ccfdba10deac724b74253b34.context: In Hadley v. Baxendale (1854), a landmark English contract law case heard before the Court of Exchequer, this chunk contains the court's holding on the rule for calculating damages in breach of contract cases. Justice Alderson establishes that damages should be limited to losses that arise naturally from the breach or were reasonably contemplated by both parties at the time of contracting, and that special circumstances unknown to the breaching party cannot form the basis for liability.

9c9444573fba2c33e9184a661bd9bcd7c1c89b68.context: This chunk from Hadley v. Baxendale (1854) presents the first count of the declaration in this landmark English contract law case heard in the Court of Exchequer. It establishes the factual background: Hadley and his partner, millers in Gloucester, hired the common carrier Pickford & Co. (the defendants Baxendale and others) to transport a broken crank shaft from their steam mill to W. Joyce & Co. engineers in Greenwich for repair, with a promised delivery date. The defendants failed to deliver the shaft on time, causing the mill to remain shut down and resulting in lost profits, which forms the basis for the damages claim in the case.
